sections.title: Level 2 Strategy
sections.content: At Level 2, the focus is on article omission and advanced conditional structures. Step 1: Identify the purpose of the noun. Step 2: Check whether an article is required or should be omitted. Step 3: Identify the type of conditional structure. Step 4: Use the correct tense and connector (if, unless, until).

sections.title: Zero Article (Primary Purpose)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify words such as school, college, hospital, prison, and bed. Step 2: Check whether the person is there for the primary purpose of that place. Step 3: If it is the primary purpose, do not use an article. Step 4: If it is used as a general place, 'the' may be used. Example: 'He is in hospital' is correct (for treatment). But 'He went to the hospital to meet his friend' uses 'the' correctly.

sections.title: Diseases, Languages, Meals, and Sports
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the noun type (disease, language, meal, or sport). Step 2: In general usage, articles are not used before them. Step 3: If there is an adjective or a specific reference, an article may be used. Example: 'She speaks English.' 'We had lunch.' 'He plays cricket.'

sections.title: Type 2 Conditional (Unreal Present)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the if-clause. Step 2: Use Simple Past tense in the if-clause. Step 3: Use would/could/might + base verb (V1) in the main clause. Step 4: This structure describes a hypothetical or unreal present situation. Example: 'If I were rich, I would travel the world.'

sections.title: Type 3 Conditional (Unreal Past)
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the if-clause. Step 2: Use Past Perfect (had + V3) in the if-clause. Step 3: Use would have + V3 in the main clause. Step 4: This structure describes a past regret or impossible past situation. Example: 'If she had studied, she would have passed the exam.'

sections.title: Use of Unless and Until
sections.content: Step 1: 'Unless' means 'if not'. Step 2: Since 'unless' already implies a negative idea, avoid double negatives. Step 3: 'Until' means 'up to a certain time'. Step 4: Check both structure and meaning carefully. Example: 'Unless you work hard, you will fail.'

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Using 'the' in primary purpose contexts. 2. Using articles before languages or meals. 3. Using present tense instead of past tense in Type 2 conditionals. 4. Forgetting 'had + V3' in Type 3 conditionals. 5. Adding an extra 'not' with 'unless'.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Zero article is used with primary purpose and general nouns. Type 2 conditionals express imaginary present situations, while Type 3 conditionals express past regret. 'Unless' means 'if not', and 'until' shows a time limit.

tricks.title: Primary Purpose Rule
tricks.explanation: For places like school, hospital, or prison, no article is used when referring to the main purpose.

tricks.title: Language Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Articles are generally not used before language names.

tricks.title: Meal Rule
tricks.explanation: Articles are usually not used with meals such as breakfast, lunch, or dinner.

tricks.title: Sports Rule
tricks.explanation: Articles are not used before the names of sports.

tricks.title: Type 2 Pattern
tricks.explanation: Remember the structure: If + past tense, would + base verb.
tricks.example: If I knew the answer, I would tell you.

tricks.title: Type 3 Pattern
tricks.explanation: Remember the structure: If + had + V3, would have + V3.
tricks.example: If he had come earlier, he would have met her.

tricks.title: Unless = If Not
tricks.explanation: Since 'unless' already means 'if not', do not add an extra 'not'.
tricks.example: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train.

tricks.title: Until Time Rule
tricks.explanation: 'Until' shows a time limit up to which something continues.

tricks.title: Meaning Check
tricks.explanation: Read the conditional carefully to determine whether it refers to an imaginary present or a past regret.
tricks.example: If I were you, I would accept the offer.
